title: Naps: Chuck's Secret Talent
summary: Josh and Chuck open with thanks for the first shows of their West Coast tour, then turn to napping. Josh admits he is a non-napper, while Chuck is a good napper. They review the stages of sleep (N1, N2, N3, REM), the grogginess of sleep inertia, and the natural internal alarm. They cover the nap definition, partial cycle (power) naps versus full cycle naps (Ed's terms), the ten-minute nap study, the coffee nap and how adenosine works with caffeine, the post-lunch dip and the best nap time near 2 pm, and adenosine as the sleepiness signal. They then weigh health effects: benefits of regular naps, a correlation between napping over an hour daily and Alzheimer's risk, genetic links to napping, and siestas across cultures. The episode closes with a listener email from Travis Wilgrin about treating his dog's rattlesnake bite with Manuka honey.

segments.title: Tour thanks and napping banter
segments.summary: Thanks to audiences at the first three tour shows in Seattle, Portland and San Francisco. Josh introduces napping and says he is a non-napper, while Chuck naps well.

segments.title: Nap definition and stages of sleep
segments.summary: The clinical definition of a nap is a sleep period under fifty percent of a person's average major sleep period. The hosts review the sleep cycle: N1, N2, N3 and REM, the cycles repeating five or six times a night, and sleep inertia after waking from N3.

segments.title: Natural alarms and waking up
segments.summary: Waking spontaneously from REM is easier than from N3. Chuck and Josh describe their internal alarms and waking before the alarm, and note that pets and children act as natural alarms.

segments.title: Partial cycle naps versus full cycle naps
segments.summary: Ed's terms: a partial cycle nap of about ten to twenty minutes ends before deep sleep, and it has the most measurable benefits. A full cycle nap runs about forty-five to ninety minutes, starting from a sixty-minute guess. A study found a ten-minute nap improved alertness and memory consolidation, and the hosts discuss napping anywhere.

segments.title: Coffee nap and the post-lunch dip
segments.summary: A coffee nap means drinking coffee and then sleeping about twenty minutes, so the caffeine wakes you as it takes effect. Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors. The post-lunch dip is a natural early-afternoon sleepiness, and a twenty-minute nap at 2 pm had greater benefits than one at noon.

segments.title: Adenosine and sleep pressure
segments.summary: Adenosine builds up as a byproduct of energy use, with ATP as the energy currency. It signals tiredness and is cleared during sleep. Adenosine is also studied as a sleep aid, but it affects heart rhythm, so it is not used that way.

segments.title: Health effects of napping, Alzheimer's, and genetics
segments.summary: Regular naps are linked with better mood, lower impulsiveness, and improved memory performance. Napping over an hour a day was correlated with a forty percent higher chance of Alzheimer's among older adults, though cause is unclear. Genome studies found 123 regions linked to daytime napping, so napping may be partly genetic.

segments.title: Siestas and cultural napping
segments.summary: Napping is not universal. Some primates, hunter-gatherer societies and cultures nap, while others do not. Spain's siesta is being abandoned, since people work late after closing for the midday break.

segments.title: Listener mail: honey saved my dog's leg
segments.summary: Travis Wilgrin of Texas writes that his chocolate lab Scout was bitten by a timber rattlesnake. Wound care with Manuka honey, after anti-venom and changes of bandage, helped the leg heal within two months.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and remind listeners how to send in stories.
